"Thumbelina" takes inspiration from the older tale "Tom Thumb".
In the first telling of the "Three Little Pigs", the wolf ate the first two pigs.
Mother Goose only appears in one nursery rhyme.
Peter Pan first appeared in a section of "The Little White Bird", a 1902 novel written by L.M.Barrie.
The moral of "Cinderella" is that beauty is a treasure, but graciousness is priceless.
When Thumbelina married the Flower-Fairy prince, he gave her a pair of fairy wings as a present.
The story of "Puss In Boots" originally comes from France.
Goldilocks didn't get her famous name until 67 years after the first Three Bears publication.
Studies have shown that children who read "The boy who cried wolf" are more likely to lie.
"Humpty Dumpty" was originally a riddle with the answer being an egg.
In early versions of "The Frog Prince", a night on the princess's pillow turned the Frog into a prince.
Several cats appear in Aesop's Fables such as "The Fox and the Cat".
The Emperor's New Clothes are invisible.
It is quite common in fairytales for cats to be able to talk, much to their owners' surprise.
The Brothers Grimm's first book of fairytales was published in 1812.
Less than 10% of fairytales feature a fairy!
A statue of the Little Mermaid sits on a rock in the Copenhagen harbor in Langelinie.
"Jack and the Beanstalk" was first told by the Vikings.
Little Bo-Peep has lost her sheep.  Reward offered. No questions asked.
Dick Whittington bought his cat for a penny which then earned him great riches.
The gingerbread house in Hansel and Gretel is not only edible but functional as well.
"Puss In Boots" was first released in 1697 and was an instant success.
In alternate versions of the tale, Goldilocks was arrested for stealing the bears' porridge!
There have been more than 50 feature films based on "Cinderella".
In the tale "The White Cat", a prince falls in love with a white cat - who is actually a princess!
In the original tale, Pinnochio rescues Geppetto from the belly of a shark.
Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!
Jumping candlesticks was once a form of fortunetelling and also a sport!
The first record of the Pied Piper was in a stained glass window in Hamelin erected in 1300.
In alternate versions of "The Frog Prince", the frog is thrown at a wall to break the curse.
Jack is the most popular boys' name found in nursery rhymes.
Cats are very rarely thwarted in their fairytale adventures.
Rapunzel was locked in her tower in the woods when she was 12.
Jack and Jill are mentioned in over 20 popular songs.
"The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs" is a fable written by Aesop over 2500 years ago!
Santa Claus and the Norse god Odin both put gifts in footwear for children.
Snow White has a sister - Rose Red.
A variant of the Gingerbread Man tale is "The Runaway Pancake".
Rapunzel is named after the Rampion Bellflower which grows mainly in Europe.
There are over 650 fables supposedly written by Aesop.
In "Beauty and the Beast", Belle's tears magically turn The Beast back into a prince!
The Brothers Grimm collected their fairytales from various storytellers and peasants.
The story of the Pied Piper is based on the real town of Hamelin where many children went missing.
"Peter Pan" was first performed as a play and then converted into a novel.
Many languages have a phrase like 'Once upon a time' to begin fairytales.
The Hansel and Gretel tale proves that putting your head in a burning hot oven is never a good idea.
Originally, Aladdin was given no limit on the number of wishes he could make!
The Ugly Duckling was just misunderstood.
In Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol", the word 'humbug' appears 8 times.
A reference to Jack and Jill can be found in Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream".
Cinderella wore sandals in the earliest version of the story.
"Jack and Jill" was originally published in "Mother Goose's Melody" in the 1760s.
"Tom Thumb" was the first fairytale printed in English.
In some fairytales, cats are beautiful princesses waiting to be returned to human form.
The Brothers Grimm's fairytales have been translated into over 160 languages.
The fairytale "Brother and Sister" is not to be confused with "Hansel and Gretel".
If you can jump over a candlestick without extinguishing the flame, it's said to be good luck.
"To cry wolf", meaning to give a false alarm, is from the fairytale "The Boy Who Cried Wolf".
In the original version, Sleeping Beauty was asleep for 100 years.
"Rumpelstiltskin" roughly translates to "Little Rattle Stilt" in German.
What will happen if Pinocchio says "My nose will grow now"? Think about it!
The line, "Fee! Fie! Foe! Fum!" can be found in Shakespeare's "King Lear".
Tom Thumb was accidently boiled into a Christmas pudding. He ate his way to freedom!
"Little Red Riding Hood" is a cautionary tale about stranger danger... and wolves.
The happy endings in fairytales have often evolved from darker endings.
Fairytales were originally for adults as much as children.
"Three Billy Goats Gruff" is a Norwegian based fairytale.
The giant in "Jack and the Beanstalk" is sometimes called "Blunderbore".
Hans Christian Andersen wrote over 30 original fairytales.
In some cultures the tooth fairy is actually a mouse!

Swipe your finger across the screen to deliciously slash and splatter fruit like a true ninja warrior. Be careful of bombs - they are explosive to touch and will put a swift end to your juicy adventure! Fruit Ninja also uses OpenFeint, so players can unlock achievements and shoot for the top of the global leaderboards while racking up OpenFeint points. Your success will also please the wise ninja Sensei, who will accompany your journey with wise words and fun fruit facts. Fruit Ninja is the messiest and most satisfying fruit game ever!
